newsitem.title: UK: Safe-haven status fails to aid Bunds amid EMU saga.
newsitem.headline: Safe-haven status fails to aid Bunds amid EMU saga.

text.p: German Bunds have profited little from speculation of a delay to European currency union, with their traditional safe haven status diminished by wider and longer-term concerns, analysts said on Wednesday.

The implications of delay on German fiscal policy, worries over a likely U.S. interest rate rise and fatter yields elsewhere in Germany have all stemmed flows into Bunds from tumbling Italian and Spanish bond markets, they said.

"Relative to other markets, Bunds would clearly benefit from a delay to monetary union becasue money would flow out of markets like Italy and back into the safe haven of Germany," said Julian Jessop, chief European economist at Nikko Securities in London. "But if monetary union is delayed that causes problems for Germany as well in two ways," he said.

Jessop said a delay to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would increase political risk because it would make Chancellor Helmut Kohl -- the driving force behind EMU -- less credible, and a win by him in 1998 elections less likely.

"The second factor is that probably fiscal policy in Germany would be less tight than it might be," Jessop said. "If they don't have to cut the deficit as much to qualify for monetary union the budget deficit will be higher, growth will likely be higher and that is a negative for Bunds."
To qualify for EMU, countries must have a deficit of no more than three percent of gross domestic product for 1997 and total public debt of no more than 60 percent of GDP.

On Tuesday Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said he did not expect Germany to meet the deficit criteria, fuelling market speculation that began earlier this year that Germany would not make the grade and EMU would be delayed.
Italian and Spanish bond markets have tumbled while German markets have slid also.
Graham McDevitt, head of bond strategy at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said the sell-off comes amid one main preoccupation for markets -- U.S. interest rates.
The Federal Reserve's policy-setting committee holds a meeting on March 25 and some economists expect a rise.

"The front end of the curve where money will be parked in a flight to safety has problems," McDevitt said. "In the last three weeks two-year yields have risen 30-odd basis points and that's been due to the market really starting to factor in there could be higher rates in the States and also that the scope for rate cuts in Germany have gone."

In addition, domestic players in Germany have are becoming more attracted to the Pfanbrief bond market where 10-year yields are now trading around 6.0 percent, slightly above Bunds at 5.89 percent, McDevitt said. The spreads between the two have also tightened over the past week, he said.
A Pfanbrief is a bond issued by authorised German banks to refinance mortgages or public projects.

Kim Thomsen, head of fixed income at Danske Invest with $250 million invested in fixed income, said talk of an EMU delay may be coming out of British financial markets but market players on the continent were still expecting EMU to start on time in 1999.
He added the Italian market has also been prey to domestic concerns. Investors are disappionted interest rates have not come down as quickly as inflation.
But McDevitt and Thomsen were divided over whether an EMU delay would benefit Bunds in the end.
"There would be a flight to safety," McDevitt said. "The current spreads on Italy and Spain still factor Italy and Spain getting in. There's still a lot of risk in those markets."
But Thomsen said there was a case to be made for avoiding the stampede into Bunds and holding out in Italy with inflation and interest rates set to fall further.
"Even 250 basis points is a very good buying opportunity for Italy," he said.
